title: An ordinary day: the four verb groups
goal: Describe your daily routine, and recognize the four Swedish verb groups from their basic form — groundwork that will make the past-tense unit later feel easy.
bekal: the four verb groups and their present-tense endings
adverbs of frequency and where they go in the sentence
describing the sequence of your day

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vad gör du en vanlig dag?
dialogs.intro: Tuesday lunchtime in the campus cafeteria. Oskar is curious how Dian organizes her days since moving to Stockholm.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Hur ser en vanlig dag ut för dig?
lines.id: What does a normal day look like for you?
lines.literal: how looks an ordinary day out for you?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag vaknar klockan sju och duschar direkt.
lines.id: I wake up at seven and shower right away.
lines.literal: I wake clock-the seven and shower directly.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.id: Do you have breakfast at home?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Alltid. Jag lagar gröt och dricker te. Sedan cyklar jag hit.
lines.id: Always. I make porridge and drink tea. Then I bike over here.
lines.literal: always. I make porridge and drink tea. then cycle I here.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.id: You bike? Even in the winter?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej! På vintern åker jag tunnelbana. Det är för kallt.
lines.id: No! In winter I take the subway. It's too cold.
lines.literal: no! on winter-the ride I subway. it is too cold.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Och på eftermiddagen? Pluggar du på biblioteket?
lines.id: And in the afternoon? Do you study at the library?
lines.literal: and on afternoon-the? study you at library-the?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Oftast. Jag läser i tre timmar, sedan handlar jag mat.
lines.id: Usually. I study for three hours, then I go grocery shopping.
lines.literal: most-often. I read for three hours, then shop I food.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.id: Don't you ever see your friends?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jo, på fredagar. Då lagar vi mat tillsammans i korridoren.
lines.id: Sure I do — on Fridays. Then we cook together in the corridor.
lines.literal: yes-indeed, on Fridays. then make we food together in corridor-the.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Det låter bra. Får jag komma på fredag?
lines.id: Sounds good. Can I come this Friday?
lines.literal: that sounds good. may I come on Friday?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Of course. We start at six.

notes: **Hur ser det ut?** — "what does it look like?". The verb is *att se ut*, "to look (out)", and its little particle *ut* always splits off and goes to the back — just like English "look *up* a word", "look it *up*". Particle verbs like this will arrive in droves at A2; for now, learn *se ut* as a single unit.

**Pluggar** is the everyday word for "studying" — the standard words are *studera* or *läsa*. Swedes say *jag pluggar svenska* far more often than *jag studerar svenska*. *Läsa* itself means both "to read" **and** "to study (a subject)": *hon läser medicin* means she's studying medicine.

**Aldrig** (never) already contains the negative, so it replaces *inte* — it isn't added to it. *Jag träffar aldrig kompisar*, not *jag träffar inte aldrig*. Exactly like standard English: "I never see friends", not "I don't never see friends".

**Handla** means shopping **for groceries or everyday necessities**. For buying one particular item, the verb is *köpa*. *Jag handlar mat* (I do the grocery shopping) vs *jag köper en bok* (I buy a book).
**Får jag…?** — "may I…?". The verb *att få* has two very different meanings: "to get" and "to be allowed to". Context separates them, and in a question it almost always means permission.

**Självklart** is pronounced **HWELV-klaht** — the *sj-* uses the breathy back sound and the *l* in *själv* is silent. It means "of course", literally "self-clear" (self-evident). Along with *absolut* and *visst*, it's the "sure, go ahead" answer you'll hear most.

grammars.title: The four verb groups
body: Every Swedish verb falls into one of four groups. The basic form decides the group, and the present-tense ending tells them apart. You don't need to memorize the past column yet — it comes in Unit 15 — but look at it now so the pattern feels familiar when the time comes.

head: Group
Base
Present
Past
Supine
Clue
rows: ends in *-a*; the biggest & most regular group
stem ends in a voiced sound (*l, m, n, r, v*)
stem ends in a voiceless sound (*k, p, s, t, x*)
one syllable, ending in a vowel other than *-a*
strong: the vowel changes, supine in *-it*

after: **Group 1 is the largest group**, and every new verb that enters Swedish goes straight into it: *att mejla*, *att googla*, *att streama*, *att fika*. If you meet an unfamiliar verb and don't know its group, treat it as group 1 — you'll be right far more often than wrong.

**The present tense has only two endings**: *-ar* for group 1, *-er* for groups 2 and 4, and just *-r* for group 3. And it's the same for every person — *jag talar, du talar, hon talar, vi talar*. No "he talks" vs "I talk". That's everything you need to master in this unit.

There are about a hundred group 4 (strong) verbs, but they include nearly all the most frequent ones: *vara, ha, gå, komma, ta, ge, se, äta, dricka, sova, skriva, sitta*. This is where English is your secret weapon: English has the same kind of list, often with the very same words — *drink-drank-drunk* runs parallel to *dricka-drack-druckit*, *sit-sat* to *sitta-satt*.

grammars.title: Adverbs of frequency, and where they go
after: Adverbs of frequency go **after the verb**, in the same slot as *inte*: *jag äter **alltid** frukost* ("I eat always breakfast"). Careful — English puts them *before* the verb ("I always eat"), so your instinct here is wrong. If you move the adverb to the front for emphasis, the verb-second rule kicks in at once: ***Ibland** tar jag bussen*.
**Ibland** and **varje dag** are the two most often moved to the front; *alltid*, *ofta* and *aldrig* usually stay after the verb.

sections.title: A day from waking up to bedtime

blocks.text: Watch out: **middag** means **dinner**, not midday — even though it looks exactly like English "midday" and literally means just that. It used to be the midday meal; over two centuries the mealtime drifted toward evening, but the name stayed put. Lunch is *lunch*, and a light evening meal is called *kvällsmat*.

blocks.title: Sequence words that tie a story together
items: **först** — first · **sedan / sen** — then · **efter det** — after that · **till slut** — finally
*Först vaknar jag, sedan duschar jag, efter det äter jag frukost, och till slut cyklar jag till skolan.*
These four words alone are enough to make your daily routine sound like a story instead of a list. And notice: **all four sit in first position, so the verb follows right behind them.**

sections.title: Which verb belongs to which group

blocks.text: Practicing how to recognize the group is more useful than memorizing it. Look at the end of the basic form, then match it up.

Group 4 verbs also end in *-er* in the present tense, so in this unit you can't tell them apart from group 2. The difference only shows up in the past tense — which is why the list of fifty verbs at the back of this module gives the past and supine forms too.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 5
items: Say the plural of these ten nouns from Unit 5 without looking: familj, bror, syster, barn, katt, hund, elev, klass, person, bok.
Then make five sentences with numbers: *Jag har tre…*, *Vi är fem…*, *Hon har tjugo…*
Finally, describe your own Tuesday in five sentences using *först, sedan, efter det, till slut*.

exercises.prompt: Write the present tense. Example: *att tala* → *talar*.

items: Han dricker ____ kaffe, för han sover dåligt.
____ tar jag bussen, men oftast cyklar jag.
Vi lagar mat ____ tillsammans på fredagar.
Hon går ____ på bio — kanske en gång om året.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: tillsammans / vi / mat / lagar / på fredagar
